title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
content: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users. It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed. Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals. One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her. The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data. Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know. "What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said. With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls. The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams. In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed. "Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said. "We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call." The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach. The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people. Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed." The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording. On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack. The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first. Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required". The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials". With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data. In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance". Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins. The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data. Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached. Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action. But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity. "Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio. "Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours." Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information". "We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said. title: Body found in Colombia in search for missing Anton Green
content: The family of a British man missing in Colombia have been told a body has been found in the search for him. Anton Green from Manchester had been living in the South American country for two-and-a-half years, but stopped responding to messages in August. Earlier, his family in Whalley Range were told that a body had been discovered, and that it was believed to be the 43-year-old. They told the BBC that the news - which came just hours after they had renewed their appeal for help finding him - had devastated them and that they were "trying to come to terms with what's happened". A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesman confirmed that the body of a British man had been found in Colombia. Anton's family had told the BBC that his failure to contact his family had been out of character. His mother, Nylva McKie-Williams, had said his last words to her in August were "we will speak at the weekend". She told BBC North West Tonight he had kept in frequent touch with his family, and that it had been "so unlike him not to be in contact with us". Last month, footballer Marcus Rashhford got behind the appeal to find him, describing him as a "family friend". Anton's brother Ro-Shaun Williams had been part of the Manchester United youth team alongside Rashford. Anton's sister Sian Tuohey described her brother as a "happy, decent guy" who had been living in Colombia for three years, having settled there while travelling. He spoke fluent Spanish and, not long before contact was lost, had moved to the Fontibon area of the capital, Bogota. The news of the discovery of a body was broken to the family by police in the early hours of Thursday, the BBC understands. His relatives said they were now waiting on more information from the Attorney General's Office in Bogota. An FCDO spokesman said: "We are aware of the death of a British national in Colombia and are providing support to their family." title: How toxic haze is causing Singapore’s landmarks to disappear
content: Indonesia is facing one of its worst wildfires seasons, with around one million hectares of land burned so far this year. title: Trump’s cheap suit is out of character and awkward for a few reasons
content: The fact that President Donald Trump was photographed flashing a suit tag from a bargain brand of imported suits should not really be news. Any woman in politics would tell you we should not dwell on how a politician dresses. But the fact that Trump, a billionaire, was photographed wearing a suit jacket with tags from Jos. A. Bank, the relatively inexpensive brand, is interesting for a number of reasons. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. Does the man who bought his own private club at Mar-a-Lago buy suits at the mall? This is the president who sells a $100,000 watch with his name on it and who allegedly inflated his net worth to be included on the Forbes list of billionaires . Status symbols are important to him. He has bedazzled the White House in gold leaf and Corinthian marble and is using taxpayer money, along with donations, to build one of the largest ballrooms on earth. All evidence suggests he likes to appear to be surrounded by the finest things. He accepted the gift of a $400 million luxury jet from Qatar to serve as his Air Force One. But he’s wearing the suit of a sensible sedan driver? The tags on Trump’s suit bear some resemblance to the Traveler collection of suit separates from Jos. A. Bank. The big and tall variant in black is currently on sale for $279 . Advertised as wrinkle- and stain-resistant, it would be a good choice for a trip across the country. Jos. A. Bank is part of a larger conglomerate, Tailored Brands, which also owns Men’s Wearhouse. The larger brand does have some products made in the US, like those from its Joseph Abboud brand, which retail for $700. Jos. A. Bank has an American Bespoke line, which is also advertised as being made in the USA, but the tags featured on the brand’s website differ from those flashed by Trump. That means Trump’s suit was likely made in China or Bangladesh — perhaps not the right message for a president who has promised the return of American manufacturing. The American-made ties by Vineyard Vines advertised on Trump’s online store retail for $125. But that’s just a tie. Just as Trump’s detractors have mocked his very long ties or the overcoat and gloves he wore to greet China’s leader Xi Jinping on a mild Washington afternoon last month, they have also seen reason to pounce on his budget-friendly suit. It’s possible Americans struggling with the affordability crisis might find the choice down-to-earth and relatable, although Trump is hardly struggling. He should be able to afford any suit he wants. His family business has seen investments in cryptocurrency pay off to the tune of more than $1 billion, according to financial disclosures . His company is selling early access to his social media posts, suggesting Wall Street firms who can afford to pay for access will want to use the information to cash in. He is pushing Americans to embrace data centers that could benefit companies in which he is invested. A conspiracy theorist like Trump could wonder if him flashing an inexpensive suit tag might be something done on purpose, to make him appear of the people. That’s been done before — think back to Al Gore’s sweaters or John Kerry’s camouflage hunting jacket or even George H. W. Bush’s cowboy boots. But it’s doubtful this was anything so calculated. Video of Trump opening his suit jacket shows that it occurred during a moment when he was dancing onstage . Taken along with the news earlier this year that Trump apparently bought Florsheim shoes , another relatively inexpensive brand of workwear, for members of his Cabinet, it may simply mean that Trump’s sartorial sensibility is mellowing with age. Trump said the Florsheim shoes were “spiffy” and an improvement over sneakers, a no-no for a Cabinet member. Back in 2016, when he was first running for president, his aide told The New York Times that Trump wore the Italian luxury brand Brioni, “among others.” Trump had previously talked about buying those suits “off the rack.” Brioni had furnished Trump’s suits during his time on The Apprentice. At the time, Trump owned a new luxury hotel in DC and Brioni had a shop there. Trump has since sold the hotel and Brioni has closed the shop. Some others might have wondered if Trump had some incentive to rep the Jos. A. Bank brand. He did, after all, sell swatches from the suit in which he posed for his mug shot in Georgia. He’s sold Bibles , watches , steaks, wine, water — you name it. But the piece of clothing that will always be most associated with Trump is the red MAGA hat, the symbol of his populist following, now for sale at his online store for $55 and made in America . CNN’s Tristen Rouse contributed to this analysis. This headline has been updated.

title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
content: Prosecutors in New York brought new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores on Thursday over the alleged torture of Americans and others who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years. They each face an additional charge of conspiracy to commit torture, according to the indictment. CNN first reported on Wednesday that the charges were expected. Prosecutors allege when Maduro became president in 2013 he “authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition,” the indictment said. Barry Pollack, Maduro’s attorney, said, “President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court.” The indictment outlines disturbing allegations of torture of both Americans and Venezuelans detained during Maduro’s time in government, including beatings, electrocutions, asphyxiation and rape. One American who was detained was allegedly forced to eat his own vomit. The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons when Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela. Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter, people briefed on the investigation told CNN Wednesday. US Attorney Jamie McDonald said at a press conference after the hearing that “Maduro, Flores and other high-ranking members of their inner circle used a violent system of torture and repression to maintain their power in Venezuela. They did this for 25 years to stifle political dissent until the US government apprehended Maduro and Flores earlier this year.” The indictment alleges “conduct that is truly unthinkable,” McDonald said. “The members of Maduro’s broad conspiracy were not just sitting behind a desk. These members of the conspiracy were holding the shovel. American citizens were tortured, and so were thousands of Venezuelans.” McDonald called the allegations “the epitome of corruption.” “This conduct, we allege, has caused significant harm to Americans, to US citizens and generational harm to Venezuelans,” McDonald said. CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores. Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York. Prosecutors said the new charges alleging “horrific” acts should be considered as a reason why Flores should not get bail. Flores appeared at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer asked that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial. The judge denied that motion, saying Flores is a flight risk and that he takes her assurances that she won’t flee with “many grains of salt.” “With all the money that’s involved and all the contacts Ms. Flores has with the Venezuelan government and the people in it, the risk is serious,” Hellerstein said. “There’s no combination that will make it less serious a risk.” If she were to escape, Venezuela probably wouldn’t extradite her back to the US to face the indictment, the judge said, adding, “there’s always ways to get out.” The defense has also argued Flores’ health is declining and that she needs to undergo treatment and convalesce outside the general population cell where she’s currently being held. Judge Hellerstein said the defense’s assertion is premature because Flores has declined to undergo certain diagnostic tests, including a cardiac catheterization. Flores has not yet been arraigned on the new conspiracy to commit torture charge unsealed in a superseding indictment Thursday before the hearing. The judge said he will post the arraignment date on the docket when it is finalized. Maduro’s lawyer is challenging the legality of the arrest and argues the former president should have immunity since the alleged conduct occurred while he was in office. The Venezuelan government is not joining in claiming immunity on his behalf, according to the prosecution. More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns. According to the indictment, one Venezuelan military officer was shocked using a live electrical wire approximately 20 times and hit on his legs, back and head with fists, belts and an object that appeared to be a pipe. The officer was hung from only his hands and feet, and waterboarded — putting his head under water to simulate drowning — about 30 times, according to prosecutors. A US citizen accused of participating in a conspiracy to assassinate Maduro was detained and tortured in January 2022, prosecutors say. He was eventually released and returned to the US in October. During his detention, “The officers punched him in the face and abdomen, covered his face, and poured a noxious liquid over his face that caused him to vomit, which the officer then forced him to eat,” the indictment said. At some point he was transferred to Boleita Norte prison for more than eight months, where he endured further torture like electrocution and forced injections the victim says caused seizures, the indictment said. “That torture included electric shock to Victim-7’s arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused Victim-? to experience seizures,” it said. He saw other Americans tortured at the prison, the indictment says. The most recent allegation of torture was in January 2025, following the presidential election, when a US citizen was arrested at his home while officials were looking for someone else. Prosecutors say the American was placed in the basement at the detention facility with a hood over his head and his hands were cuffed behind his back. Over two days, the indictment alleges, he was beaten hourly in the head, stomach and face, resulting in permanent injury to his eye. Several Americans detained by the Maduro government have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained. Heath told CNN on Thursday the new charges against Maduro and his wife feel “like justice is being served.” The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. In lawsuits filed against their employer — Citgo — Tomeu Vadell, Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned. Maduro and his wife shifted blame on the instability in Venezuela onto the United States resulting in the detention of the six oil executives — including five Americans. The Citgo-6 were detained in Venezuela and charged with corruption in 2017. After that, authorities allege the abuse of American citizens by Venezuelans authorities increased. All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report. That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.” María Oropeza, state coordinator of the Vente Venezuela party, responded to the anticipated new charges over the alleged torture of Americans. “This is good news for those of us who want justice, not so much for those who still believe that they will return,” she wrote on X. “I only hope that someday they will face charges for torturing Venezuelans.” This story was updated with additional information. CNN’s Michael Rios and Lauren del Valle contributed to this report.

title: An Ohio edge. An Iowa tossup. New CNN polls give Democrats hope in a pair of red states
content: Widespread dissatisfaction with the state of the country has opened up a prime Senate pickup opportunity for Democrats in Ohio and made for a razor-thin contest in Iowa , according to new CNN polls conducted by SSRS. President Donald Trump carried both states by double digits in 2024 , and Republicans currently hold both US Senate seats and complete control of the state government in each of them. But in these deep-red states, likely voters now mostly disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, say his policies have increased the cost of living and that tariffs on foreign goods have largely been a negative for their states. About four in 10 in each state say they are financially worse off than they were two years ago. Asked which party they’d like to see in control of the Senate after this year’s midterms, Iowa’s likely voters favor the Republicans (53% to 46%). In Ohio, it’s a more even divide (52% Democrats, 48% Republicans). And in both states, Democrats have the upper hand in the race for governor. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown holds a 6-point lead among likely voters over Jon Husted, a Republican former lieutenant governor who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Brown is more widely known and better liked than Husted, according to the poll, and voters on both sides of the contest say their decision is more about Brown than it is about Husted. Nearly half of likely voters see Brown’s views and policies as about right ideologically, while 43% call him too liberal. Fewer are satisfied with Husted’s positions – 42% call his views and policies about right, 40% say he’s too conservative and 16% not conservative enough. Among Brown’s own supporters, 62% say that choice is more a vote for Brown than against Husted, and likewise, Husted’s voters are more anti-Brown voters (56%) than pro-Husted voters (44%). About 4 in 10 likely voters in Ohio say that which party controls the Senate will be more of a factor in their vote than the candidates’ experience and character or their positions on the issues. Voters motivated by that are split about evenly between Brown and Husted. In order to take control of the Senate, Democrats need to hold their seats in battlegrounds like Michigan, New Hampshire and Georgia while flipping four seats currently held by Republicans. The party’s best pickup opportunity comes in North Carolina, but Ohio may be their next best shot. Iowa, one of several deeply red states at the heart of this year’s Senate playing field , is more of a stretch for Democrats. The poll finds no clear leader in the Senate race in Iowa, with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson at 45% to Democrat Josh Turek’s 43% among likely voters. Almost 3 in 10 Iowa likely voters say they haven’t yet firmly decided whom to support, and sizable shares don’t yet have an opinion on each candidate. Turek is less well-known than Hinson, with 24% saying they have never heard of him or don’t have an opinion, while 18% say the same about her. Those with an opinion of Hinson break more negative than positive, while views of Turek are about evenly split. In contrast with Ohio, most backers of both candidates in Iowa say their choices are motivated by support for their chosen candidate rather than by opposition to their opponent: 66% of Hinson supporters and 60% of Turek supporters say their choice is in support of their candidate. There are some signs in the poll that Iowa offers a better playing field for Republicans than does Ohio. In addition to likely voters’ preference for a GOP-controlled Senate, Trump’s approval rating here stands at 41% compared with 36% in Ohio and notably above his 34% average nationwide in the CNN Poll of Polls . And in assessing the candidates, more call Turek too liberal (46%) than say that Hinson is too conservative (38%). In both Iowa and Ohio, about half of likely voters call the economy and cost of living their top issue, more than 20 points higher than the second most important issue, the state of US democracy. The economic concerns that have buffeted Trump’s approval ratings nationally all year long are evident here. About three-quarters in each state say that Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living there, majorities say that increased tariffs on foreign goods are a bad thing for their state and roughly seven in 10 say they have faced at least some hardship from rising gas prices. Overall, far more say their own financial situation has worsened in the last two years than say it has gotten better. About four in 10 in each state say they are angry about the way things are going in the country today. Those angry voters express more motivation to vote than do those who are enthusiastic or satisfied with the way things are going in the country in both states. In both states, Democrats lead in the race for governor among likely voters. Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in Iowa by 9 points, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton tops Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 8 points. Both would be Democratic pickups if these margins were to hold. Impressions of Ramaswamy and Lahn appear to be weighing down their candidacies, with the share of likely voters who hold unfavorable opinions of the two Republicans outpacing favorable views by double-digit margins. By comparison, nearly half of Iowa likely voters have a favorable view of Sand – compared to 32% unfavorable – while in Ohio views of Acton are more evenly split. CNN’s Ariel Edwards-Levy, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.

title: Trump says he will not attack Iran before the midterm election
content: President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm election. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon. The president’s comments come after multiple media reports detailed the administration planning for potential new strikes before the elections — just 26 days away. Trump emphasized that he plans to keep up economic pressure on Iran, saying the blockade of Iranian ports “will remain in full force and effect.” The administration has favored economic punishment over military strikes for months, though it’s seemingly done little to motivate Iranian officials to negotiate. The Treasury Department announced additional sanctions against Iran on Thursday, impacting 17 vessels that officials alleged were part of a “shadow fleet” that Iran has used to ship its oil around the world. The department concluded that they had circumvented existing US sanctions to transport millions of barrels of oil and other petrochemical products to countries across south and east Asia. “Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said in its statement announcing the new sanctions. Trump has suggested in campaign trail remarks over the last several weeks that he is considering new military action on Iran, telling supporters he has a decision in front of him on how to proceed. While other administration officials have claimed the war is essentially over, Trump said this week the US still has unfinished business. “They’re a mess. But we still have to finish it off,” he said during remarks at a new shipyard in Maryland on Tuesday. The US president has appeared reluctant to resume the war in earnest before the midterms, however, mindful of the political downsides that could come with renewing an already unpopular conflict. Officials also know that flareups between the US and Iran have caused spikes in oil prices, aggravating cost-of-living concerns that have dragged down Trump’s Republican allies. Still, the president had not entirely ruled out resuming military strikes before the midterms until his post on social media Thursday, according to officials familiar with the matter. They said American military planners have been preparing options for a resumption of hostilities, including targeting Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear targets. Trump and top national security officials have held extensive discussions about the next steps in Iran as they work to find a way to get more ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Top administration officials traveled to Camp David last Friday for a discussion on Iran, including longer-term planning on the war, officials said. Trump’s claim of “productive discussions” with Iran came after the president rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last month. Since then, the US has sent a counterproposal that Tehran says it is considering. An Iranian news agency reported Thursday that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said officials planned to respond “within the next few days.” This story has been updated with additional reporting and developments.

title: Trump admin bars Microsoft and other tech companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers
content: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and some other companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers hired through the H-1B visa program, accusing them of taking advantage of the process so that they could replace American citizens with cheaper labor from abroad. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the tech giant is one of a handful of companies to be barred indefinitely from the Labor Department’s PERM program following an investigation spearheaded by the anti-fraud task force that he chairs. That probe determined that Microsoft laid off roughly 6,000 American workers last year, while at the same time employing 6,300 non-citizens that it had brought to the US by obtaining H-1B visas for them. “The H-1B visa is how the people get into the United States in the first place, and then a PERM program is how those employees stay,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.” Vance and other top administration officials alleged that Microsoft had misrepresented its needs in applying for permanent residency for its foreign workers, arguing that the program is meant only for workers with “hyper-specialized” skill sets that can’t be easily found in the US. Instead, they accused the company of using the program primarily to replace skilled American employees with similarly qualified immigrants who it could pay less to do the same job. “The fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal,” Vance said. In a post on its website , Microsoft officials disputed Vance’s assertions, saying that 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications the company submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new ones. The rest of its applications were for people hired by the company who were already legally in the US. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings,” Microsoft officials wrote. “We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” The announcement also raised immediate questions about the timing of the administration’s targeting of Microsoft. In a separate ceremony on Thursday, President Donald Trump is due to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The medal is the nation’s highest honor for technological achievement and is awarded to those who make “outstanding contributions to America’s economic, environmental and social well-being,” according to the US Patent and Trademark Office. Vance downplayed the administration’s decision to punish Microsoft over accusations of fraud on the same day that it hailed the company’s achievements. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company, it’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans,” he said. “So we’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” The Labor Department is also indefinitely suspending software firm Adobe and several IT outsourcing firms from the PERM program, meaning that any new or pending requests for permanent residency for their workers will not be considered. Vance did not lay out any specific steps for the companies to regain access to the process, saying only that it wanted Microsoft and others to “change their behavior, improve their behavior and actually get better.” The move marks the Trump administration’s latest attempt to show it’s cracking down on instances of government “fraud” ahead of the midterm elections, framing the issue as critical to ensuring Americans have fair access to job opportunities and federal benefits. Trump officials on Thursday also announced that they planned to separately investigate several universities over allegations of that they had abused the J-1 visa program, which allows them to bring in foreign nationals as students, researchers or teachers. Under that program, Vance said, officials believe that schools regularly employ workers from abroad as a way to undercut the salaries that they would otherwise need to pay to Americans in those positions. The universities under scrutiny are Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; California Institute of Technology; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; and Arizona State University. This story was updated with additional information.

title: ‘I don’t love that’: Vance signals discomfort after report alleges ambassador sought funds for access to Trump administration
content: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he took issue with anyone seeking financial gain in exchange for access to Trump administration officials after a report claimed Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, sought funds and offered access to top administration officials ahead of her confirmation. “Obviously I don’t love that,” Vance said when a reporter asked whether he had any reaction to a scenario where an American ambassador tried to exchange access for funds. The reporter did not name Guilfoyle specifically. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle had asked a donor and former congressional candidate for $100,000 to pay off an American Express bill. CNN has reached out to Guilfoyle. A lawyer for the ambassador told the Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages. Vance, who said he was unsure of the specifics of the episode, reserved further comment during a press conference on visa fraud. But the vice president said in general he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes. “Of course I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” he said. “But you know, I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of of the way you’re describing it,” he added. According to the Journal, the donor, Eric Deters, had been seeking Guilfoyle’s help in “getting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues.” “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle texted Deters days ahead of her confirmation hearing, according to the Journal. Deters didn’t make the payment, the newspaper reported. Guilfoyle had been with Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he visited Greece and gave a major policy speech this week. When asked about the Journal reporting earlier on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said before he boarded his plane to leave the country, with Guilfoyle looking on. Guilfoyle was nominated to the role in Athens by President Donald Trump in December 2024, prior to him taking office. She had been engaged to Donald Trump Jr. and is close to the Trump family. Guilfoyle is a former co-host of Fox News’ “The Five” and was an assistant district attorney at the San Francisco and Los Angeles district attorneys’ offices before beginning her media career. She abruptly left her position on Fox News in July 2018 and later served as the Trump campaign’s finance chair during his 2020 presidential bid. She later became a key witness to the events leading up to the US Capitol attack on January 6, 2021, and met with the House select committee investigating the insurrection in 2022. In addition to her role on Trump’s campaign, Guilfoyle also helped raise money for organizers leading up to the “Stop the Steal” rally on January 6. This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Marco Rubio uses a dramatic backdrop to sketch a post-MAGA foreign policy
content: In the golden light of an Athens evening, with the Acropolis over his shoulder, Marco Rubio hardly looked like a man planning to ride off into a political sunset. The secretary of state’s speech in Greece on Wednesday will surely reignite speculation around his future presidential intentions. It implicitly positioned him as both the heir to and the modernizer of the “America First” movement — just weeks before the 2028 race roars into life after the midterm elections. Rubio depicted the West as a continuous inheritance dating from Ancient Greece to modern America, epitomizing “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention” as well as duty and heroism. But he warned that the civilization, ashamed of its achievements and embarrassed by its past, risked “atrophy, servitude and decline.” “Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” Rubio said, giving himself some political cover for the high-profile appearance. One interpretation is that this was yet another bid to retroactively impose doctrinal coherence on Trump’s erratic foreign policy of Iran war-style gut calls, power grabs and a transactional approach to resources. And Rubio is just the latest administration official to bemoan Europe’s supposed decline; failure to tackle mass immigration; and prioritization of the “global community” over national interest. This canon was hallmarked by Vice President JD Vance’s stemwinder in Munich last year. Yet he was seeking something deeper, at times, sketching the framework of a post-MAGA foreign policy in which US sovereignty and action remain paramount, while​ reinvigorating friendships shattered by Trump’s hostility. “We must rebuild our institutions and alliances” to face new great power rivalries and respond to a “new universe” of threats and attacks, Rubio said. His comments also reinforced a message to decayed European militaries that the US now expects alliances to offer tangible military multipliers to Washington. It was a hint that while nothing will be the same after Trump, a future Republican president might still value updated transatlantic ties. Rubio also seemed to be fusing three strands of traditional GOP foreign policy — the muscular internationalism of Ronald Reagan, the realism of Richard Nixon and Trump’s coercive nationalism. He might also have been trying to make sense of his own political evolution from aspirational conservatism to his current, darker worldview. (Rubio’s critics portray his conversion to MAGAism as the cynical act of a political chameleon desperate for power.) The speech was also jarring and contradictory. He was the latest Trump acolyte to travel to Europe to explain Europe’s history to Europeans and to adopt an idealized view of Western civilization that fits the needs of America’s Christian nationalist right. When Rubio laments eroded national sovereignty, like Vance, he seems oblivious to enduring national and cultural differences distinguishing French, German, Italian, and other European citizens. He ignored gruesome history that led late 20th-century leaders to constrain raging nationalism within shared political and economic structures. And while Trump’s team believes something is rotten in Europe, many Europeans perceive a corrupt and increasingly authoritarian American is most to blame for obliterating Western values. Noting that “passions” have rocked the alliance, Rubio used a deceptive euphemism for Trump’s bullying. Rubio’s lionizing of the ancient Greeks as foundational to the US also overlooked the founders’ concern that their direct democracy encouraged factionalism and promoted demagogues. Their answer was the Electoral College. Some Europeans will be offended by Rubio’s speech. But he’s seen by allies as the most conventional and sympathetic Trump foreign policy official, so his comments may be less provocative than rebukes by Vance or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Inevitably, such an ambitious speech using the optics of a major campaign address will stir presidential speculation. Visually, Rubio’s setting recalled then-Sen. Barack Obama’s hilltop speech at the Citadel in Amman, Jordan, in 2008. A Rubio run in 2028 seems problematic with Vance in pole position as the vice president. But whether he next takes aim at the White House in two years, in 2032, or later, Rubio showed the world Wednesday his ambition is unquenched.

title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
content: Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel , with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton. The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed. The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.” Miliband said the mission remained independent, by which he meant it will continue to report directly to the UK Foreign Office in London rather than through the UK embassy in Tel Aviv. One former Foreign Office diplomat said: “Israel has always wanted to shut the consulates in Jerusalem […] Israel will come for the French next.” Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.” He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’ ”. Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that, having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months. He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, in effect suspending discussions until a new Israeli government is formed. UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and that it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome. The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. It was thought not feasible to defy Israel since the UK diplomats would have no security protection. Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal. Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.” Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute. The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this. The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the UN and most of its members as being occupied Palestinian territory. Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them. UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, as Britain has become increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seems prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments have thought is unachievable through his methods. The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this a matter for international courts to determine.

title: French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU
content: The French finance minister has invited the UK to “come all the way back” to the European Union after Andy Burnham raised the prospect of a new referendum to reverse Brexit. Roland Lescure was speaking after the prime minister used his Labour conference speech to pledge that the government would explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year. He used subsequent interviews to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”. Asked about Burnham’s comments, Lescure told the BBC: “British people decided, and that’s obviously their 100% right, and if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide. But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime.” Lescure said he wanted Britain back in the union to face emerging global threats together. Burnham said last week that the government’s options included keeping the current arrangements in relation to the UK’s relationship with the EU, seeking a customs union, returning to the single market, or going “all the way” with full membership. He said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option. The prime minister is travelling to Germany for talks with the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose government has been supportive of Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could explore closer links with the EU. Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Burnham and Merz are expected to agree on a deal for closer security cooperation against cyber-attacks on European countries but the two will also discuss UK-EU relations. Lescure also responded to comments by Burnham that EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK. British government sources warned days earlier that the “EU reset” summit would be delayed again unless the bloc agreed to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. “Come back, and you’ll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together,” Lescure said. Nigel Farage has claimed Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate , which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage said: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.”

title: Voting opens in high-stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection
content: Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection , a contest seen as a key gauge of Andy Burnham’s ability to energise voters and whether Zack Polanski’s Greens can still peel off support from Labour’s left. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister. The seat is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold. Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes. Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign . He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat. However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour. Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies . Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party. Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party. While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning. The stakes are also high for Burnham. Failure to win the seat by a reasonable margin could end his honeymoon period and bring renewed doubts about Labour’s ability to protect inner-city seats from the Greens, who won several London councils in May’s local elections.
